blocks.text: Lion is a comparatively newer optimizer, discovered through an automated search process rather than hand designed, that updates weights based only on the sign of the momentum direction rather than its full magnitude, resulting in a simpler update rule and a smaller memory footprint than Adam.

This topic covers what makes Lion structurally different from the Adam family of optimizers covered earlier in this module, and the practical considerations worth knowing before adopting it for a fine-tuning project.
1. What Lion Stands For and Where It Came From

blocks.alt: What Lion Stands For and Where It Came From
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101173-97822916.png

Lion, short for Evolved Sign Momentum, was found through a large scale automated search over possible optimizer designs, rather than being manually derived the way earlier optimizers like Adam were, an unusual origin that reflects a broader trend of using automated search to discover effective machine learning components.
2. Sign Based Updates, The Core Idea

blocks.alt: Sign Based Updates, The Core Idea
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101174-746438754.png

Rather than scaling its update by the actual magnitude of the gradient or momentum, as Adam does, Lion looks only at the sign, positive or negative, of the momentum direction, applying the same fixed step size regardless of how large or small the underlying gradient signal actually was.
3. Lion vs Adam, A Structural Comparison

blocks.alt: Lion vs Adam, A Structural Comparison
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101174-857443153.png

Adam, covered in the earlier Optimizers topic, carefully scales its updates based on both the direction and the magnitude of recent gradients, while Lion deliberately discards magnitude information, using only direction, a simpler design that surprisingly performs competitively on several benchmarks despite throwing away information Adam relies on.
4. Memory Savings From Lion's Simpler State

blocks.alt: Memory Savings From Lion's Simpler State
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101175-105406224.png

Because Lion only needs to track one momentum term per parameter, rather than the two separate running estimates Adam maintains, covered further in the Optimizer States topic, its memory footprint is smaller than Adam, though not quite as dramatically reduced as the factoring approach Adafactor uses.

blocks.text: 5. Lion's Sensitivity to Learning Rate
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101176-738336263.png

Because Lion updates use a fixed step size regardless of gradient magnitude, its effective update size behaves differently than Adam, and practitioners commonly need to use a noticeably smaller learning rate with Lion than they would with AdamW for a comparable training setup, a detail worth checking carefully rather than reusing an AdamW tuned learning rate directly.

blocks.title: Do not reuse an AdamW learning rate value directly with Lion
blocks.content: Because the two optimizers scale their updates so differently, a learning rate well tuned for AdamW is very likely to be inappropriate, often too large, if applied directly to Lion without adjustment.

blocks.text: 6. When Lion Has Shown Strong Results

blocks.alt: When Lion Has Shown Strong Results
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101176-32073818.png

Lion has shown particularly strong reported results on certain large scale vision and language tasks in published research, sometimes matching or slightly outperforming AdamW while using somewhat less memory, though results across different tasks and model sizes vary enough that it is worth testing empirically rather than assuming it will always outperform AdamW.
7. Lion's Adoption Relative to AdamW

Despite promising results, AdamW remains far more widely used and battle tested across the fine-tuning ecosystem covered throughout this course, and Lion adoption, while growing, is still comparatively niche, worth trying specifically when a team has the bandwidth to experiment and compare rather than as an unquestioned default replacement.
8. Practical Considerations Before Switching to Lion

blocks.alt: Practical Considerations Before Switching to Lion
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101177-338755118.png

Before adopting Lion for a real fine-tuning project, running a direct comparison against an AdamW baseline on the actual task at hand, with appropriately adjusted learning rates for each, gives a much more reliable signal than assuming published results on a different task and model will transfer directly.
9. Lion in the Broader Optimizer Landscape

Lion, Adafactor, and AdamW together illustrate a genuine spectrum of tradeoffs covered across this module, AdamW as the well tested, widely supported default, Adafactor trading precision for memory efficiency at scale, and Lion trading Adam adaptive magnitude scaling for an even simpler, memory lighter update rule.
Worked Example

A team curious about Lion runs a direct comparison against their existing AdamW baseline for the same fine-tuning task, carefully searching for an appropriate, smaller learning rate for Lion rather than reusing their AdamW value directly.

They find Lion reaches a comparable final loss with a slightly smaller memory footprint, confirming it as a viable alternative for their specific setup, though they note the result required careful learning rate tuning rather than working well out of the box with their existing AdamW configuration.
Common Mistakes

items: Reusing an AdamW tuned learning rate directly with Lion without adjusting for its different update scaling behavior
Assuming Lion will automatically outperform AdamW based on published results from a different task or model
Switching to Lion for a project where its memory savings over AdamW were never actually a meaningful constraint
Not running a direct empirical comparison before adopting Lion for a production fine-tuning workflow

blocks.text: Practice

In your own words, explain why an optimizer that uses only the sign of the gradient direction, discarding its magnitude, would likely need a different, probably smaller, learning rate than one that scales its updates based on full gradient magnitude the way Adam does.
Key Takeaway

Lion updates weights using only the sign of the momentum direction rather than its full magnitude, a simpler mechanism discovered through automated search that reduces memory overhead compared to Adam, but it requires careful, separately tuned learning rate selection and empirical comparison against AdamW before adopting it for a real fine-tuning project.
